A summary with a quiz, then decision situations and 40 true/false statements.
Which is not a limitation of pile driving?

In rock, hard (stony) clay, strongly cemented soil and fill with large blocks the pile cannot be driven – often even a thin such intercalation stops it. In loose and medium-dense sand driving (vibrating) works well, and the displacement even compacts the soil.
Which technology is chosen specifically where noise and vibration are restricted?
CFA is made by drilling, it is low in noise and vibration, and it progresses fast. Driven and vibrated piles, and ramming the Franki pile, come with significant noise and vibration.
A pile 120 cm in diameter and 35 m long is needed in silty soil with a high water content. Which is the safe choice?

The casing supports the wall of the bore until concreting, so it is safe even in silty soil with a high water content; it is made with diameters of 80–180 cm and lengths of 15–50 (100) m. CFA is at most 22–24 m.
When is a well foundation economical?
If the bearing stratum is not too deep and the groundwater is high
If the bearing stratum is 40 m deep
If a foundation has to be taken into rock without vibration
If we are founding a lightweight house

A well foundation is typically 4–8 m long and 0.8–3.0 m in diameter; it is competitive with piles if the bearing stratum is not too deep, especially with high groundwater, when the foundation level has to be taken below the water table.
A diaphragm wall has to be taken into rock. What would you excavate the trench with?

In rock and very hard clay a diaphragm wall can only be built with a hydrofraise (a reverse-circulation trench cutter with cutter wheels). It is very expensive, but it gives an accurate trench to great depth, in any soil and rock.
In which soil is trench stability difficult to ensure?
In peat, soft clay, flowing sand
In dense sandy gravel above the groundwater
In hard clay above the groundwater
In medium-dense sand with deep groundwater
In soft clay, peat, flowing (submerged) sand and with a very high groundwater table, the slurry can hardly support the wall of the trench – in such cases the diaphragm wall reaches its limits.
Where are ground screws typically used?
Under solar parks, fences, lightweight houses
Under the river pier of a long-span bridge
As the watertight side wall of an underground car park
For the 40 m deep foundation of a tower
The ground screw is for founding lightly loaded structures; it is typically at most 2–3 m long, can be installed by machine or by hand, and is easy to recover – also for temporary, mobile structures.
In which soil is the cast-in-place (displacement) screw pile not suitable?
In rock, a very dense, hard layer

The displacement drilling head works well in loose to medium-dense granular, intermediate and soft–firm cohesive soil: it pushes aside and compacts the soil. It cannot penetrate a hard, very dense layer.
Which statement is true of large-diameter piles (above 80 cm)?
They are made exclusively with replacement technology
They are made mainly precast and driven
They can only be ground screws
They are always made of timber
Piles with a diameter above 80 cm are made exclusively with replacement technology – by cased or bentonite-supported drilling, or with a larger CFA rig.

Why go deep? – scour around a bridge pier

The strip footing of the old masonry wall is overloaded: the pressure under the footing on the soft layer is high, the wall has settled and cracked – or storeys are to be added, which would bring even more load. The bearing stratum lies deeper.

The small drilling rig fits into the cellar. They drill obliquely down through the existing footing to the bearing stratum; along the wall the inclination of the piles alternates. No driving, no vibration – the house can remain occupied.
A steel core is placed in the bore (or the hollow drill rod stays in), and the grout is injected from the bottom up. In the bearing stratum the cement body and the permeated, rough sleeve form.

The upper part of the pile is bonded to the old structure by grouting within the existing footing (with a new reinforced concrete capping beam if needed). It is often preloaded with a jack so that the load is transferred immediately.

The micropiles transfer the load of the wall to the bearing stratum along their shafts – no base resistance is assumed. The pressure under the old footing decreases and the settlement stops; the basement can even be deepened.

Illustrative figure, with distorted scale: in reality the micropiles are typically 6–15 m long, closely spaced along the wall, with alternating inclination. How the load is shared between the footing and the piles depends on the preloading and on further settlement.

The soil is so soft (or the free length so long) that the pile already buckles at ${fmt(R.Ncr, 0)} kN – before it reaches its resistance of 130–180 kN. Then buckling must be checked separately: a stiffer core, a larger cement body, or eliminating the free length helps.

The critical force (${fmt(R.Ncr, 0)} kN) falls within the 130–180 kN resistance band: the pile cannot be used up to its full resistance. A stiffer core, the support of the cement body, or a shorter free length helps.

c<sub>u</sub> < 10 kPa: buckling must be checked separately. In this model the critical force (${fmt(R.Ncr, 0)} kN) is still above 180 kN, but cracking of the cement body or a small cavity quickly reverses this.

The critical force (${fmt(R.Ncr, 0)} kN) is greater than the resistance of 130–180 kN: the lateral support is enough, so the shaft resistance governs, not buckling. Switch off the stiffness of the cement body, or add a free length – and watch the curve!

The returning spoil cannot escape to the surface along the hole: the pressure of the 400–600 bar jet builds up in the soil. The soil fractures, and the surface – and the neighbouring building – may be lifted. The outflow of spoil must be watched all the time!

The column spacing (${fmt(s, 2)} m) is not smaller than the diameter (approx. ${fmt(D, 2)} m): the columns do not intersect, and the wall is not watertight. Reduce the spacing or increase the diameter.
At the overlap the wall is only approx. ${fmt(t, 2)} m thick. A 1 % drilling deviation already means 10 cm at a depth of 10 m – deeper down a gap can easily open.
A lift of ${fmt(R.dz, 1)} cm per revolution is too much: the jet does not “sweep” the whole shaft, and untreated soil may remain in the column along a helix. Slow down or rotate faster.

What is the maximum shaft diameter of a bored micropile?
The shaft diameter of a bored micropile is at most 250–300 mm; the 150 mm limit applies to the largest cross-sectional dimension of a driven micropile.
What is neglected when calculating the resistance of a slender micropile?
soft clay, silt: 10–25 kPa; very soft, organic soil: below 10 kPa
